newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin says NATO act binding, gives Russia say.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin says NATO act binding, gives Russia say.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin said the deal Russia struck with NATO on Wednesday would be binding on the western alliance and that it would give Moscow the means to block any decision by NATO it did not approve of.

In an interview on Russian Television, Yeltsin said that Russia was still opposed to NATO's expansion into eastern Europe but foresaw "calm" relations after a planned May 27 signing of the binding NATO-Russia Founding Act.

"The binding nature of this document is clear to see," Yeltsin said, saying the Act would be similar to the 1975 Helsinki Act. That was not ratified by national parliaments -- the usual mark of a binding treaty under international law -- but governments which approved it regard it as an obligation.

"Decisions can be taken only by consensus," Yeltsin said of NATO decisions following the signing of the Act. "If Russia is against some decision, it means this decision will not go through. That is of capital importance."
The Kremlin leader also indicated NATO may have given pledges not to deploy forces in the territories of those former Soviet-bloc states likely to be given membership shortly.

"If military forces are not to be deployed in the new member states, then this is to be precisely observed," he said. It was not clear if he was referring to Russian demands or the actual treaty contents. "Nuclear weapons are not to be deployed, no storage facilities are to be used, infrastructure abandoned by the Warsaw Pact is not to be used," Yeltsin added.
